tasks.summary: This is the tile-size planner in a blocked matrix-multiply pipeline; it decides what Tm/Tn/Tk block sizes to run the loop nest with for `C=A*B`, which directly determines how many bytes have to be moved from DRAM. The existing `plan_tiling` runs but chooses poorly — you must pick, from the candidate sizes on each axis, the combination that minimizes memory traffic. The input is a batch of multiply tasks (M/N/K, element byte size, and the allowed tile candidates per axis) plus an on-chip buffer cap; the output is the `[Tm,Tn,Tk]` for each task. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 63.46): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is one training step of a SwiGLU gated feed-forward block; the naive approach keeps every intermediate activation around for the backward pass, so peak memory runs very high. The `gated_mlp_fwd_bwd` in `submission/kernel.py` is empty (it just raises) — you must implement both the forward and the backward pass and use chunked recomputation to bring the memory high-water mark down. The input is the activation x, three weight matrices, the upstream gradient, and `chunk_size`; the output is the forward result y and the gradient dx with respect to x. Metric: binary implementation-class score — 1.0 only if all hidden cases and hard gates pass; any single case failure or a triggered forbidden-edit/cheat condition is 0.0, with no partial credit.

This is the metadata-merge step of a distributed checkpoint: each rank writes out the metadata for its own shard, and these must be aggregated into the global checkpoint metadata. `merge_shard_extents` is empty — per the contract, you must compute for each logical tensor the maximum byte boundary covered by all of its shards (i.e. the total flattened size), and do it fast. The input is the shard-metadata records from each rank; the output is a mapping from each tensor name to its global total size. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 41666.7): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the reuse layer of a batch-execution service: before running an expensive step, it computes a short string identity for the request signature and reuses the previous result on a hit. The existing `identity_key` is correct but produces far more distinct identities than necessary (equivalent requests compute different keys, needlessly losing cache hits) — you must canonicalize it and speed it up. The input is a structured signature dict; the output is a short string, where equivalent signatures must yield the same string and inequivalent ones must never collide. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 4): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the gradient-exchange path of data-parallel training, running over a bandwidth-limited network; right now every step ships the full-precision, whole gradient block and saturates the link. You must rework `compress`/`decompress` so that the payload actually put on the wire each step is far smaller, while using error feedback to keep long-run training unbiased. The input is this step's gradient buffer (plus the error state carried across steps); the output is the compressed payload and the decompressed gradient usable for the update. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 31.7519): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the attention step in the transformer stack of a high-throughput inference service, computing causally-masked scaled dot-product attention over the entire input sequence. The existing `causal_attention` is a naive implementation (it materializes the whole attention matrix) — you must rewrite it in a blocked, online-softmax style. The input is q/k/v, the scaling factor, and the causal flag; the output is the probability-weighted average over value for each query position. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 6): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the half-precision dense matrix multiply at the core of an inference service's linear layer — a CUDA kernel, with Tensor Cores available underneath but going unused. You may only modify `gemm_kernel.cu`; you must make the fp16 GEMM fast using the Tensor Core MMA instructions, and you are forbidden from delegating to a ready-made library such as cuBLAS. The input is two fp16 matrices A(M,K) and B(K,N); the output is C(M,N), and it must accumulate in float32 internally. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 2): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the graph-fusion pass in a tensor-program AOT compiler: once the model has been lowered to a DAG, it must be rewritten — before being handed to codegen — into an equivalent graph with fewer nodes. You must collapse recognized numerical idioms into a single fused operator and delete redundant pass-through nodes, so that downstream launches fewer kernels, while also speeding up the pass itself. The input is an operator DAG; the output is a semantically equivalent DAG with fewer nodes. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 11.2917): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is a data-layout kernel used all over an inference service: transposing a row-major matrix, in a GPU CUDA implementation. You may only modify `transpose_kernel.cu`; you must make it fast via coalesced memory access plus vectorization (e.g. shared-memory tiling to avoid non-coalesced writes), and you are forbidden from calling a framework built-in transpose. The input is x(M,N); the output is y(N,M) with y[j,i]==x[i,j], and it must match element-for-element exactly. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 3.16): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the memory pool of a training runtime: it carves many variable-length buffers out of one reserved arena, and each buffer must occupy contiguous cells. After a long run of allocations and frees the arena fragments — you must speed up the pool's logic for coalescing free blocks and compacting (sliding live buffers toward the front). The input is a stream of allocate/free operations; the output is the offset of each allocation (plus the post-compaction layout), and the behavior must match the reference implementation. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 3.01623): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the inner product of block-encoded integer vectors, the basic building block of block-quantized matrix-vector multiply, running on CPU. The existing `blocked_dot` is correct but slow — you must vectorize it for speed while keeping bit-for-bit identical results. The input is two block-encoded vector streams (each with its accompanying coefficients/signs); the output is their integer inner product. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 1.25313): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the index-arithmetic frontend of a kernel code generator: after a tensor program is lowered to a loop nest, every memory access turns into a mechanically-generated, often bloated integer index expression. You must speed up this simplifier, rewriting each expression into a smaller canonical form that computes the same integer for every value the variables can take. The input is an index expression and the lower/upper bounds of each variable; the output is an equivalent, simplified expression. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 3.36): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the loss stage of a large-model training step: computing the mean cross-entropy over a batch of logits and integer labels, along with its gradient with respect to the logits. The existing implementation runs in multiple passes (softmax first, then the gradient) — you must fuse it into a single pass to cut memory round-trips. The input is logits(N,V) and labels(N) (which may contain ignore labels); the output is the scalar loss and a gradient with the same shape as logits. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 7.4157): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the data-movement frontend of a chunked GPU workload in an inference service: a large tensor is already sliced into N row-chunks in host memory, and each chunk must be moved to device memory and then computed. The existing `streamed_chunk_apply` does a serial copy-compute-copy — you must use multiple CUDA streams to overlap the H2D copies with computation. The input is the list of chunks on the host and a per-chunk GPU compute function; the output is a single device tensor concatenated back in the original order. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 1.4856): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the reuse layer of a batch build service: before running an expensive compile, it computes a short identity for the build-spec and reuses the already-produced artifact on a hit. The existing `identity_key` produces far more distinct identities than necessary (equivalent specs compute different keys) — you must canonicalize it and speed it up. The input is a build-spec dict; the output is a short string identity, where semantically equivalent specs must share a key and inequivalent ones must never collide. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 4): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is a linear layer with a small low-rank correction — the LoRA structure used for cheap adaptation of large models. The existing `lowrank_adapter_apply` computes the base multiply and the low-rank correction separately, with redundant intermediate materialization — you must speed it up while staying within numerical tolerance. The input is x, the frozen base weights, and two low-rank factors (with scale); the output is `y = x@W^T + scale*((x@A^T)@B^T)`. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 1.1626): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the zero-order-hold (ZOH) discretization step in a Mamba/state-space model, converting continuous-time parameters into the discrete recurrence coefficients used at each step. The `discretize` in `submission/kernel.py` is empty — you must implement it correctly per the contract (this task judges correctness only, not speed). The input is the continuous parameters A/B and the step size delta; the output is the discretized A_bar/B_bar, and it must genuinely depend on the input. Metric: binary implementation-class score — 1.0 only if all hidden cases and hard gates pass; any single case failure or a triggered forbidden-edit/cheat condition is 0.0, with no partial credit.

This is chunked-attention merging in a high-throughput inference server: the KV of a long sequence is split into several disjoint chunks that are computed separately, each producing a partial output and the log-sum-exp of that chunk's softmax. You must accelerate combine_attn_states, recombining these partial results into a single output equivalent to running attention over the full sequence at once. The inputs are partial_out(N,R,D) and partial_lse(N,R), and the outputs are the merged out and lse. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 6.4424): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the metric-aggregation path of an observability platform: individual services report sparsely-stored exponential-bucket histograms (native histograms) that must be folded into a single aggregated result. You must accelerate this merger so that it is fast in the common case of sparse buckets and a very wide dynamic range, while producing results identical to accumulating them one by one. The input is a stream of sparse histograms (carrying only non-empty buckets, along with their schema and sum), and the output is a single merged histogram. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 2.58717): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the core operator of an S4-style long-convolution sequence model: a causal convolution of the sequence with a very long kernel. The causal_conv in submission/kernel.py is empty, and you must implement it (this task only checks correctness): it must be strictly causal and may not read future samples. The input is a sequence x and a long convolution kernel, and the output is the causal-convolution result of the same length. Metric: binary implementation-class score — 1.0 only if all hidden cases and hard gates pass; any single case failure or a triggered forbidden-edit/cheat condition is 0.0, with no partial credit.

This is a single-precision dense matrix-multiply (SGEMM) CUDA kernel for the linear layers of an inference server. You may only modify sgemm_kernel.cu, and must make it fast using register-level tiling (each thread computes multiple outputs); delegating to an off-the-shelf BLAS library is forbidden. The inputs are A(M,K), B(K,N), C(M,N) and alpha/beta, and the output is D = alpha*A@B + beta*C. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 2.99): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is a caching allocator in a training runtime: device-memory allocation and deallocation are expensive, so freed buffers first go into a pool and are reused directly by the next request of the same size. The existing CachingAllocator is correct but slow, and you must accelerate it while preserving exactly the same allocation/reuse/eviction behavior. The input is a stream of alloc/free requests with a capacity limit, and the output is the disposition of each request (which block was reused, whether a new allocation was made, whether an eviction occurred). Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 25.4863): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is a matrix-multiply kernel for the linear layers of an inference server, where the difficulty is insufficient parallelism on tall-skinny shapes (M and N very small while K is enormous). You may only modify gemm_kernel.cu, and must make such shapes fast using split-K (splitting the K dimension into segments computed in parallel and then reduced); delegating to an off-the-shelf library is forbidden. The inputs are A(M,K) and B(K,N), and the output is C(M,N), including extreme long-inner-product cases with M=N=1. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 5.69): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the per-row sequence-mixing step inside a high-throughput sequence-model block on GPU, essentially a short-window causal depthwise 1D convolution plus gating. You must accelerate channel_window_op: a trailing-window weighted sum along the length axis, adding a per-row bias, then applying a smooth gating activation. The inputs are x(B,C,L), per-row weights w(C,K) and an optional bias, and the output is y of the same shape and dtype. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 18.5413): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is a sequence-mixing layer in a long-context language model: it mixes tokens using a continuously-updated small state matrix together with per-feature decay gates, as a replacement for pairwise attention. The existing implementation advances the state serially, one timestep at a time, and you must rewrite it into a chunked form to make it fast. The inputs are the per-step q/k/v and decay gates, and the output is the step-by-step output stream (including the final state when required). Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 62.2504): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the core sequence operator of a state-space / linear-recurrence block: it advances a hidden state with a first-order linear recurrence along the time axis and reads it out step by step. The existing state_space_scan is serial and step-by-step, and you must parallelize it (e.g. chunking / prefix scan) to speed it up while preserving its numerical behavior. The inputs are A(B,L,D,N), B(B,L,N), C(B,L,N), x(B,L,D), and the output is y(B,L,D). Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 103.182): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the forward path of multi-scale retention (RetNet) in the real open-source repository fla-org/flash-linear-attention (an LLM-infra kernel library with 2000+ GitHub stars). The in-scope implementation is correct but very slow — it advances the retention state serially in Python, one timestep at a time, and you must rewrite it into a chunked parallel implementation. The inputs are q/k/v and a fixed per-head exponential decay, and the output is the attention output of chunk_retention (the public signature may not be changed). Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 510.24): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is a selector that picks cloud instance types for a batch of resource requests: the catalog is a flat table of (cloud, region, instance type) carrying vCPU/memory/accelerators and both on-demand and spot prices. The existing implementation linearly scans the whole table for every request, and you must make batch selection fast while preserving exactly the same selection results. The input is the catalog table and a batch of resource requests (minimum vCPU/memory, accelerator kind and count, billing mode, budget), and the output is the instance type chosen for each request. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 5.95969): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is communication-chunk balancing in DiLoCo-style low-frequency-communication training: split a batch of tensors to be synchronized into P chunks so that the byte size of the largest chunk is as small as possible (bottleneck minimization). The balance_chunks in submission/kernel.py is empty, and you must implement it and make it fast. The input is the byte size of each tensor and the chunk count P, and the output is the chunking plan; scoring is based on the ratio of your largest chunk's bytes relative to the oracle. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 1.66973): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the admission step of a tiered KV cache offloading policy (TinyLFU style): a candidate block is promoted only if the frequency sketch judges it hot enough and it is not already present downstream. select_offload is empty, and you must implement the admission decision using a count-min sketch (a [D,W] count table with D independent hash rows) and make it fast. The input is the list of candidate blocks, the sketch count table, and the set already present downstream, and the output is the list of blocks admitted for offload. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 12.4236): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the name-routing step of a multi-file mmap weight loader: several shard files declare, in order, the tensor names they contain, and for a tensor name that appears more than once the last file to declare it wins. resolve_tensor_files is empty, and you must implement this last-write-wins routing and make it fast. The input is the list of tensor names declared by each shard file and a batch of tensor names to look up, and the output is which file each name should be fetched from. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 12195.1): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is all-to-all redistribution in tensor-parallel / expert-parallel setups: rearranging data distributed under one sharding scheme into another. The routine in submission/kernel.py is empty, and you must implement the redistribution and make it as fast as possible on GPU (H20). The input is the sharded data under the source sharding and a description of the target sharding, and the output is the shards under the target sharding; the score is dominated by the largest-scale mesh. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 1428.57): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the load-balancing routing core of a serving system: each request gives you two candidate replicas, and by the power-of-two-choices rule you send it to whichever currently has the lower load, then update the bookkeeping. route_p2c is empty, and you must implement this rule and make batch routing fast. The input is the replica count R, the two candidates for each request, and the initial loads, and the output is where each request lands (along with the updated loads). Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 2.93589): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is runtime memory planning: assign offsets within a single arena to a batch of buffers that have lifetime intervals, where buffers with overlapping lifetimes may not overlap in memory. plan_arena is empty, and you must implement a legal and as-compact-as-possible plan, and make the planning process itself fast. The input is each buffer's size and its [alloc, free) lifetime, and the output is each buffer's arena offset (legality is a hard gate). Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 5.68182): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the fair-scheduling step of a multi-tenant serving scheduler (VTC-style fairness: one bursty tenant must not starve its neighbors). fair_interleave_order is empty; you must implement a round-robin interleaving order across tenants (every tenant's 1st item, then every tenant's 2nd item, …) and make it fast. The input is the pending service queue ordered by arrival (tagged with tenant id), and the output is the interleaved service order. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 43.0923): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the commit step of speculative decoding: after the target model has verified a batch of draft trees, the accepted prefix of each request must be moved from the draft staging slots into that request's own paged KV table. The existing implementation is slow; you must accelerate this transfer plan — each request has a different accepted length, so the plan is ragged, not a simple memcpy. The inputs are the post-verification accepted lengths, the draft staging slot positions, and each request's paged KV table; the output is the slot transfer plan/result. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 4.89637): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the gradient-clipping step of the training loop: all gradients are scaled by the same factor so that the L2 norm of all gradients concatenated together is bounded. clip_grads_by_global_norm is empty; you must implement it and make it fast on the GPU (H20) (avoiding many per-tensor kernel launches). The inputs are a list of gradient tensors and a norm upper bound; the output is the in-place clipped gradients (covering both the clip-triggered and not-triggered cases). Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 8.20708): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the post-processing after all-reduce in tensor parallelism: the partial sums from each rank are reduced and then a bias is added, and the two steps can be fused. reduce_partials is empty; you must implement the reduce-plus-bias and make it fast on the GPU (H20). The inputs are the partial results from each rank and the bias; the output is the reduced-and-biased tensor. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 7.8501): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is group-relative advantage estimation in RL post-training (verl-style): the multiple responses sampled from the same prompt form a group, and each sample's advantage must be normalized relative to its own group. You must implement two estimators, GRPO and RLOO (this task only judges correctness, with binary scoring). The inputs are token-level rewards (B,L), the response mask, and the grouping index; the outputs are the advantages and returns for each sample. Metric: binary implementation-class score — 1.0 only if all hidden cases and hard gates pass; any single case failure or a triggered forbidden-edit/cheat condition is 0.0, with no partial credit.

This is the hot path of RDMA transfer: before sending bytes, two questions must be answered — which registered memory region this address falls in, and which pre-sliced block tier (8KiB/64KiB/2MiB) this size should be sent from. The in-scope implementation is correct but slow (linearly scanning registered regions, advancing byte by byte); you must make these two lookups fast while preserving all behavior bit-for-bit, including the roughly seventy kinds of ValueError. The input is a stream of address and payload-size queries; the output is the matched registered region and the allocated block. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 3.76753): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is ColossalAI's device-mesh communication-group planner: devices are arranged on an N-dimensional logical mesh, and for a given device you must return the list of collinear devices along each mesh axis. The in-scope implementation is correct but slow — when it back-computes mesh coordinates into a global device id, it scans through all devices; you must make it fast. The inputs are the mesh shape and the device number; the output is the communication-group member list along each axis for that device. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 7.00536): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the difficulty-cluster selection of DeepSpeed-style curriculum learning: according to the current curriculum stage, the batch to use is picked from the sample difficulty clusters. You may only edit curriculum_cluster.py; you must find the slow points within scope and drive down the wall-clock time of select_curriculum_cluster. The inputs are the difficulty-cluster structure and the curriculum parameters; the output is the set of selected sample indices. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 20.777): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the empirical-complexity estimator in a microbenchmark framework, corresponding to Google Benchmark's ComputeBigO / MinimalLeastSq (src/complexity.cc). The existing implementation uses naive least squares to fit each candidate curve one by one and is slow; you must accelerate it while keeping the fitting result bit-for-bit identical. The input is a set of (workload size, measured run time) pairs; the output is the best-fit complexity curve and its leading coefficient. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 55.6106): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the per-counter finalization of a microbenchmark framework, corresponding to Google Benchmark's Finish (src/counter.cc) and the flag semantics of counter.h. The existing implementation is slow; once iterations/cpu_time/num_threads are known, you must convert each counter's raw value into its final value according to that counter's flag bits, and make this step fast. The input is a batch of counters carrying raw accumulated values and flag bits; the output is the converted final values (a single mismatch means a score of 0). Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 15.1272): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the MoE routing-preprocessing subsystem of NVIDIA Megatron-LM: it turns the token dispatcher's per-token expert selection into the dense structure that the downstream grouped computation consumes. Two operators run back to back (converting compact expert indices into a dense multi-hot routing map, then doing an index transformation); you must make them fast (Triton fusion is allowed). The inputs are the per-token expert indices and probabilities; the outputs are the dense routing map over the local experts and the transformed indices. Metric: continuous performance-class score — first pass a hard correctness gate, then score on a logarithmic curve relative to the oracle anchor (ref_speedup = 5.90276): tying the anchor scores 0, you must exceed it to score anything, and reaching the anchor squared caps at 1.0.

This is the MoE routing-map alignment padding of Megatron-LM: to align the expert GEMM, the number of tokens assigned to each expert must be padded up to some multiple. The in-scope implementation scans the routing map item by item in Python and is slow; you must vectorize it for speed, and the result must match (turning the earliest unassigned entries into assigned ones).
